title: Remark
body_md:
Consider the following two-state continuous-time Markov chain in standard form:
$$Q=\begin{bmatrix}
    -1 & 1\\
    1 & -1
\end{bmatrix}.$$
This transition rate matrix can be obtained from the following positive transition rate matrix and its associated negative transition rate matrix:
$$Q^+ = \begin{bmatrix}
    1 & 1\\
    1 & 1
\end{bmatrix},\\
Q^- = \begin{bmatrix}
    -2 & 0\\
    0 & -2
\end{bmatrix}.$$
Here, it is easy to see that the two states are in some way ``equivalent", in that they transition back to themselves and to each other at the same rate, but this information gets lost in the standard form. This notion of equivalence will be rigorously developed in \autoref{paper2:model:ctmdp:theory}.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
For any finite-state finite-action CTMDP with self-transitions, with vector costs $\bm{c}(s,a)$ and generalised transition rates $q^+$, we say that two state-action pairs $(s,a)$ and $(s',a')$ are:
    \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
        \item \emph{stochastically equivalent} if  $q^+(s,a,s'') = q^+(s',a',s'')$ for all states $s''$, and write $(s,a)\sim^{q^+} (s',a')$,
        \item \emph{cost equivalent} if $\bm{c}(s,a)=\bm{c}(s',a')$, and write $(s,a)\sim^{\bm{c}}(s',a')$,
        \item \emph{totally equivalent} if $(s,a)\sim^{q^+} (s',a')$ and $(s,a)\sim^c(s',a')$, and write $(s,a)\sim (s',a')$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Additionally, for any DS policy $\mu$, we say that two states $s,s'$ are:
    \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
        \item \emph{stochastically equivalent} if $(s,\mu(s))\sim^{q^+}(s',\mu(s'))$, and write $s\sim_\mu^{q^+}s'$,
        \item \emph{cost equivalent} if $(s,\mu(s))\sim^{\bm{c}}(s',\mu(s'))$, and write $s\sim_\mu^{\bm{c}}s'$,
        \item \emph{totally equivalent} if $(s,\mu(s))\sim(s',\mu(s'))$, and write $s\sim_\mu s'$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Finally, for any equivalence relation $R$ over the feasible state-action space $\mathcal{SA}$ and any DS policy $\mu$, we can define the \emph{$\mu$-adapted equivalence relation} $R_\mu$ over the state space $\mathcal{S}$ as $s\,R_\mu\,s' \iff (s,\mu(s))\,R\,(s',\mu(s'))$

title: Definition
body_md: Let $\mu$ be a DS policy for an impulsive CTMDP. Let $\{s_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ be the sequence of states defined by $s_1=s$ and $s_{n} = s_{n-1}\oplus\mu(s_{n-1})$ for $n\geq 2$. Let $\{a_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ be the sequence of actions defined by $a_n=\mu(s_n)$. We call $\{a_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ the \emph{chain of $s$ under $\mu$}, and denote it by $\text{Chain}^\mu(s)$. We call $\{s_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ the \emph{state chain of $s$ under $\mu$}. We also define the \emph{degree} of a chain by the number of non-zero actions in the chain.

label: lemma:OneStepSequencingIsOptimal
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:OneStepSequencingIsOptimal}
    Let $Q^*$ be the optimal $Q$ value function for a single-objective impulsive CTMDP. If $a_1\neq0$ is optimal for some state $s$ and $a_2\neq0$ is optimal for $s\oplus a_1$, then $a_1\oplus a_2$ is also optimal for $s$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Suppose that there exists a state $s$ such that $s,a_1,a_2$ are as described. By optimality, $Q^*(s,a_1)\leq Q^*(s,a)$ for all states $s$ and actions $a$. For any such $s$, we have $Q^*(s\oplus a_1,0) = Q^*(s,a_1) \leq Q^*(s, a_1\oplus a_2) = Q^*(s\oplus a_1 \oplus a_2,0)$. However, because $a_2$ is optimal for $s\oplus a_1$, we also have $Q^*(s\oplus a_1 \oplus a_2,0) = Q^*(s\oplus a_1, a_2) \leq Q^*(s\oplus a_1, 0)$. Therefore $Q^*(s\oplus a_1,0) = Q^*(s\oplus a_1 \oplus a_2,0)$ and hence $Q^*(s,a_1) = Q^*(s,a_1 \oplus a_2)$, so action $a_1\oplus a_2$ is also optimal for $s$.
head: environment

label: prop:sequencedOptimalPoliciesAreOptimal
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:sequencedOptimalPoliciesAreOptimal}    
Let $\mu$ be an optimal policy. Then $\text{Seq}_k\{\mu\}$ is an optimal policy for all $k$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: We proceed by induction. It is immediate from \autoref{lemma:OneStepSequencingIsOptimal} that $\text{Seq}_1\{\mu\}$ is optimal. Now assume $\text{Seq}_k\{\mu\}$ is optimal for some $k$. It follows that for any state $s$, $\text{Seq}_k\{\mu\}(s)$ is optimal for $s$ and $\mu(s\oplus\text{Seq}_k\{\mu\}(s))$ is optimal for $s\oplus\text{Seq}_k\{\mu\}(s)$. Hence, by \autoref{lemma:OneStepSequencingIsOptimal}, $\text{Seq}_k\{\mu\}(s)\oplus\mu(s\oplus\text{Seq}_k\{\mu\}(s))$ is also optimal for $s$, so by definition $\text{Seq}_{k+1}\{\mu\}(s)$ is optimal for $s$. Therefore, $\text{Seq}_{k+1}\{\mu\}$ is also an optimal policy.
head: environment

label: prop:loopBreakingIsOptimal
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:loopBreakingIsOptimal}
    Let $\mu$ be an optimal policy for an impulsive CTMDP, and let $s$ be a looping state with respect to $\mu$. Then action $0$ is optimal for $s$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: If $s$ is a looping state, then it reappears at some index $n>1$ in its state chain, so $s\oplus a_1\oplus\dots\oplus a_{n-1} = s$ and therefore $a_1\oplus\dots\oplus a_{n-1} = 0$. Action $a_1\oplus\dots\oplus a_{n-1}$ is also optimal for $s$ because $\text{Seq}_{n-2}\{\mu\}$ is an optimal policy. Therefore 0 is optimal for $s$.
head: environment

body_md:
\label{coro:aggregatedChainsAreOptimal}
    Let $\mu$ be an optimal policy with no looping states, so all chains have a finite number of non-zero actions. Then, for any state $s$, $a_1\oplus\dots\oplus a_{N(s)}$ is optimal for state $s$, where the $a_n$ form the chain of $s$ with degree $N(s)$.

title: Definition
body_md: For any impulsive CTMDP, we say two feasible state-action pairs $(s_1,a_1),(s_2,a_2)\in\mathcal{SA}$ are \emph{impulsively equivalent} if $s_1\oplus a_1 = s_2\oplus a_2$, and write $(s_1,a_1)\sim_\oplus(s_2,a_2)$. For an impulsive CTMDP controlled by a DS policy $\mu$, we say two states $s_1$ and $s_2$ are \emph{impulsively equivalent} if $(s_1,\mu(s_1))\sim_\oplus(s_2,\mu(s_2))$, and write $s_1\sim_{\oplus\mu} s_2.$

name: Impulsive Equivalence

title: Example
body_md:
Consider a controlled impulsive CTMDP with state space $\mathcal{S} = \{1,2,3,4\}$ and action spaces:
    $$\mathcal{A}(1) = \mathcal{A}(2) = \{0,1\},\, \mathcal{A}(3) = \mathcal{A}(4) = {0}.$$
    Let $\mu(1) = \mu(2) = 1$, $1\oplus1 = 3$ and $2\oplus 1 = 4$. Suppose all costs are 0, so all states are trivially cost equivalent. Suppose $q^+(3,0,3) = q^+(3,0,4) = q^+(4,0,3) = q^+(4,0,4) = 1$. Then all states are stochastically equivalent under $\mu$ and hence are all equivalent under $\mu$. However, state-action pairs $(1,1)$ and $(2,1)$ are not impulsively equivalent because $1\oplus1\neq2\oplus1$.

label: lemma:coherenceImpliesRelated
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:coherenceImpliesRelated}
    Let $\mu$ be a coherent policy. Then $s\sim_{\oplus\mu}s\oplus\mu(s)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: We see that $(s,\mu(s))\sim_\oplus (s\oplus\mu(s),0) = (s\oplus\mu(s), \mu(s\oplus\mu(s)))$, so $s\sim_{\oplus\mu}s\oplus(\mu(s))$.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: Let $\mu$ be a coherent policy, and let $\widehat{s}$ be an equivalence class with respect to $\sim_{\oplus\mu}$. There is exactly one $s\in\widehat{s}$ such that $\mu(s) = 0$, which we call the \emph{post-decision state} of the class.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: We first prove existence of such a state. The class $\widehat{s}$ is a non-empty set and therefore contains some state $s'$. It follows that either $\mu(s')=0$, so such a state exists, or $\mu(s')\neq 0$ and therefore the class also contains $s'\oplus\mu(s')$ by \autoref{lemma:coherenceImpliesRelated}, which by definition of coherence satisfies $\mu(s'\oplus\mu(s')) = 0$. To show uniqueness, suppose there exist two states $s_1,s_2\in\widehat{s}$ such that $\mu(s_1)=\mu(s_2)=0$. Then since $s_1\sim_{\oplus\mu}s_2$ we have $(s_1,\mu(s_1))\sim_\oplus (s_2,\mu(s_2))$ and hence $(s_1,0)\sim_\oplus(s_2,0)$. Therefore $s_1\oplus0=s_2\oplus0$, implying that $s_1=s_2$.

name: Cost-Free Direct Product of Impulsive CTMDPs

title: Remark
body_md: {\color{black} A subtlety of this definition is that compartments are not entirely stochastically independent, even if ``controlled separately'' (which we will define shortly). Consider a two-compartment product impulsive CTMDP in state $\bm{s}=(s_1,s_2)$ under non-zero action $\bm{a}=(a_1,a_2)$. By definition, we have that $q^+(\bm{s},\bm{a},\bm{s}')=q^+(\bm{s}\oplus\bm{a},\bm{s}')$, so all possible next states are of the form $(s_1\oplus a_1,s_2')$ or $(s_1',s_2\oplus a_2)$. This means that an ``event'' in one compartment triggers all other compartments to simultaneously transition to ``remember'' the action that was previously being applied. Despite this apparent implicit dependence between compartment processes, we will later prove, under suitable conditions, that the controlled product processes still decompose into separate independent processes.}
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: An impulsive CTMDP $$\mathfrak{C} = \langle\mathcal{S},\left(\mathcal{A}(s)\right)_{s\in\mathcal{S}}, q^+:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}, \bm{c}:\mathcal{SA}\to\mathbb{R}^k, \oplus:\mathcal{SA}\to\mathcal{S}\rangle$$is called \emph{stochastically decomposable with $I$ compartments} if the tuple $\langle\mathcal{S},\left(\mathcal{A}(s)\right)_{s\in\mathcal{S}}, q^+, \oplus\rangle$ can be expressed as a cost-free direct product of impulsive CTMDPs $\{\mathfrak{C}_i\}_{i=1}^I$. A choice of such sub-CTMDPs then gives the \emph{compartments} of the stochastically decomposable impulsive CTMDP.
head: environment
name: Stochastic Decomposability

title: Definition
body_md: Let $\mu$ be a DS policy for a stochastically decomposable impulsive CTMDP with compartments $\{\mathfrak{C}_i\}_{i=1}^I$. We say that $\mu$ is a \emph{separable policy} if there exist functions $\mu_i$ such that, for all $\bm{s}\in\mathcal{S}$, we can write $\mu(\bm{s}) = (\mu_1([\bm{s}]_1), \mu_2([\bm{s}]_2),\dots, \mu_I([\bm{s}]_I))$. That is, the action taken on compartment $i$ depends only on the state of compartment $i$.
head: environment
name: Separable Policy

title: Remark
body_md: The flexibility of separable policies relies on the \emph{choice} of decomposition. As such, we advise caution when considering the choice of decomposition when limiting to such policies. It is not always necessarily best to decompose a problem as much as possible, as heuristics based on the use of separable policies may sometimes perform better when certain compartments are left non-decomposed.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $\mathfrak{C}$ be a stochastically decomposable impulsive CTMDP with $I$ compartments and $K$ objectives. Let $\bm{g}:[0,1]^{|\mathcal{SA}|}\to\mathbb{R}^K, \bm{g}(\pi) = \sum_{s\in\mathcal{S},a\in\mathcal{A}(s)}\bm{c}(s\oplus a)\pi(s,a)$ be the function mapping every solution of OP to its long-run average cost. The cost function $c_k:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R}$ is a \emph{decomposable cost function} if there exists a {\color{black}component-wise strictly} increasing function $f_k:\mathbb{R}^I\to\mathbb{R}$ and functions $c_{i,k}:\mathcal{S}_i\to\mathbb{R}$ for $i\in\{1,\dots,I\}$, which we call the \emph{$k$th sub-state costs}, such that for every $\bm{\pi}$ corresponding to a coherent separable policy $\mu$, we have:
    $$g_k(\pi) = f_k\left(\sum_{(s_1,a_1)\in\mathcal{SA}_1}c_{1,k}(s_1\oplus a_1)\pi_1(s_1,a_1),\dots,\sum_{(s_I,a_I)\in\mathcal{SA}_I}c_{I,k}(s_I\oplus a_I)\pi_I(s_I,a_I)\right),$$
    where $\pi_i(s_i,a_i) := \sum_{\bm{s},\bm{a}:[\bm{s},\bm{a}]_i = (s_i,a_i)}\pi(\bm{s},\bm{a})$ is the probability that compartment $i$ is in sub-state $s_i$ and undergoing sub-action $a_i$.
head: environment
name: Decomposable Cost Function

title: Remark
body_md:
We may write the right-hand-side of the above expression in shorthand form as:
    $$f_k\left(\left(\sum_{(s_i,a_i)\in\mathcal{SA}_i}c_{i,k}(s_i\oplus a_i)\pi_i(s_i,a_i)\right)_{i=1}^I\right).$$

label: lemma:coherentIffSubCoherent
title: Lemma
body_md: A separable policy $\mu$ is coherent if and only if each subpolicy $\mu_i$ is coherent. \label{lemma:coherentIffSubCoherent}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mu$ be coherent and separable, so there exist policies $\mu_i:\mathcal{S}_i\to\mathcal{A}_i$ such that $\mu(\bm{s}) = (\mu_1([\bm{s}]_1),\dots,\mu_I([\bm{s}]_I))$ for all $i$. We also have that $\mu(\bm{s}\oplus\mu(\bm{s})) = 0$ for all $s$. Now:
    \begin{align*}
        \mu(\bm{s}\oplus\mu(\bm{s})) = \bm{0} \text{ for all }\bm{s}&\iff [\mu(\bm{s}\oplus\mu(\bm{s}))]_i = 0\text{ for all }\bm{s},i\\
        &\iff 
        \mu_i([\bm{s}\oplus\mu(\bm{s})]_i) = 0 \text{ for all }\bm{s},i\\
        &\iff \mu_i([\bm{s}]_i\oplus \mu_i([\bm{s}]_i)) = 0 \text{ for all }\bm{s},i\\
                                                                                                      
        &\iff \mu_i(v\oplus\mu_i(v)) = 0\text{ for all }i, v\in\mathcal{S}_i.
    \end{align*}
    So the bi-implication holds.

label: lemma:state-action-equiv
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:state-action-equiv}
    Let $(\bm{s}_1,\bm{a}_1),(\bm{s}_2,\bm{a}_2)\in\mathcal{S}\mathcal{A}$ be two state-action pairs of a decomposable impulsive CTMDP. Then $([\bm{s}_1]_i,[\bm{a}_1]_i) \sim_{\oplus_i} ([\bm{s}_2]_i,[\bm{a}_2]_i)$ for all $i$ if and only if $(\bm{s}_1,\bm{a}_1) \sim_{\oplus} (\bm{s}_2,\bm{a}_2)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: We have $([\bm{s}_1]_i,[\bm{a}_1]_i) \sim_{\oplus_i} ([\bm{s}_2]_i,[\bm{a}_2]_i)$ for all $i$ if and only if $[\bm{s}_1]_i\oplus [\bm{a}_1]_i = [\bm{s}_2]_i\oplus [\bm{a}_2]_i$ for all $i$, which holds if and only if $\bm{s}_1\oplus \bm{a}_1 = \bm{s}_2\oplus \bm{a}_2$, which is identical to $(s_1,a_1)\sim_{\oplus}(s_2,a_2)$ by definition.

label: prop:sequencedBoundsGetWorse
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:sequencedBoundsGetWorse}
    Let $\mu^*$ be an average-optimal policy for an impulsive CTMDP. Let $J^{\mu^*}_t$ be the finite-horizon value function under policy $\mu^*$ for state $s$ until time $t$. Assume $t>T$ for some $T$ large enough that $\mu^*$ is $t$-optimal for all $t>T$, and $T\geq t(s,a)$ for all $s,a$. Let $Q^{\mu^*}_t$ be the action value function. Let $a_1\neq0$ be an action for state $s$ satisfying $Q^{\mu^*}_t(s,a_1)= (1+\varepsilon(t))J^{\mu^*}_t(s)$ for some $\varepsilon(t)\geq0$, and let $a_2\neq0$ be an action for $s\oplus a_1$ satisfying $Q^{\mu^*}_t(s\oplus a_1,a_2) = (1+\varepsilon'(t))J^{\mu^*}_t(s\oplus a_1)$ for some $\varepsilon'(t)\geq0$. Then $Q^{\mu^*}_t(s,a_1\oplus a_2) \leq (1 + \varepsilon(t))(1+\varepsilon'(t))J^{\mu^*}_t(s)$. Additionally, there exist cases where this bound is tight.

body_md: Let $\widehat{(\bm{s},\bm{a})}\in\widehat{\mathcal{SA}}$, and choose any $(\bm{s}_1,\bm{a}_1),(\bm{s}_2,\bm{a}_2)\in\widehat{(\bm{s},\bm{a})}$. By \autoref{lemma:state-action-equiv}, we have $[\bm{s}_1,\bm{a}_1]_i\sim_{\oplus_i}[\bm{s}_2,\bm{a}_2]_i$ for every $i$, so $\varphi_i([\bm{s}_1,\bm{a}_1]_i) = \varphi_i([\bm{s}_2,\bm{a}_2]_i)$ for every $i$. Therefore any $\widehat{(\bm{s},\bm{a})}\in\widehat{\mathcal{SA}}$ can be mapped to exactly one member of $\widehat{\mathcal{SA}_i}$ for every $i$, and we can denote this by $\psi_i(\widehat{(\bm{s},\bm{a})})$.

body_md: For each $i$, there exists a projection $\psi^\mu_i:\widehat{\mathcal{S}}\to\widehat{\mathcal{S}_i}$ such that for every $\widehat{\bm{s}}\in\widehat{\mathcal{S}}$ and $\bm{s}\in\widehat{\bm{s}}$, $\varphi^\mu_i([\bm{s}]_i) = \psi^\mu_i(\widehat{\bm{s}})$.

label: prop:CS-MILP_to_DC-MIP
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:CS-MILP_to_DC-MIP}
    Let $\mathfrak{C}$ be a decomposable impulsive CTMDP, and choose a decomposition into compartments $\{\mathfrak{C}_i\}_{i=1}^I$. Let $(\bm{\pi},\bm{y})$ be a solution to CS-MILP for $\mathfrak{C}$. Then there exists a solution $\{\bm{\pi}_i,\bm{y}_i\}_{i=1}^I$ for DC-MIP with compartments $\{\mathfrak{C}_i\}_{i=1}^I$ satisfying the equations \eqref{eq-whole-to-compartment-decision-vars} and \eqref{eq-compartment-to-whole-decision-vars}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
$\pi(\bm{s},\bm{a})$ is a basic feasible solution of OP for $\mathfrak{C}$, and corresponds to a deterministic policy $\mu(\bm{s}) = \arg\max_{\bm{a}\in\mathcal{A}(\bm{s})}\pi(\bm{s},\bm{a})$. Moreover, by the separable and coherent constraints, $\mu$ must be a separable and coherent policy. Therefore, $\mu$ can be written as $(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_I)$ where the $\mu_i$ are coherent policies for the compartments $\mathfrak{C}_i$. Now, let $V^{\mu_i}$ be the stationary distribution of the CTMC defined by compartment $\mathfrak{C}_i$ as controlled by policy $\mu_i$, for each $i$. Then: $$\pi_i(v,b) := \begin{cases}
     \mathbb{P}(V^{\mu_i} = v),& b = \mu_i(v)  \\
     0, & otherwise, 
\end{cases}.$$
provides a basic feasible solution for OP for $\mathcal{C}_i$, satisfies the equivalent constraints in DC-MIP, and satisfies \eqref{eq-whole-to-compartment-decision-vars} and \eqref{eq-compartment-to-whole-decision-vars}. If we let $y_i(v,b) = \mathbb{I}\{b=\mu_i(v)\}$ for all $i$, and recall that the $\mu_i$ are coherent, then $\{\bm{\pi}_i,\bm{y}_i\}_{i=1}^I$ provides a feasible solution to DC-MIP.

label: prop:DC-MIP_to_CS-MILP
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:DC-MIP_to_CS-MILP}
Let $\mathfrak{C}$ be a decomposable impulsive CTMDP, and choose a decomposition into compartments $\{\mathfrak{C}_i\}_{i=1}^I$. Let $\{\bm{\pi}_i,\bm{y}_i\}_{i=1}^I$ be a solution to DC-MIP for compartments $\{\mathfrak{C}_i\}_{i=1}^I$. Then there exists a solution $(\bm{\pi},\bm{y})$ to CS-MILP for $\mathfrak{C}$ satisfying \eqref{eq-whole-to-compartment-decision-vars} and \eqref{eq-compartment-to-whole-decision-vars}.

title: Proof
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We must show that the existence of a solution with a certain objective value in one of the problems implies the existence of a solution in the other problem with the same objective value.

First, let $(\bm{\pi},\bm{y})$ be a solution to CS-MILP. We want to show that it has a corresponding solution in DC-MIP with the same objective value. The solution $(\bm{\pi},\bm{y})$ can be mapped to a solution $(\bm{\pi}_i,\bm{y}_i)_{i=1}^I$ of DC-MIP by \autoref{prop:CS-MILP_to_DC-MIP}, with $\bm{\pi}$ and $\bm{\pi}_i$ related by \eqref{eq-whole-to-compartment-decision-vars} and \eqref{eq-compartment-to-whole-decision-vars}. We recall:
$$g_k(\bm{\pi}) = f_k\left(\left(\sum_{s_1,a_1\in\mathcal{SA}_1}c_{1,k}(s_1\oplus a_1)\pi_1(s_1,a_1)\right)_{i=1}^I\right),$$
and we need only focus on one entry in this, so for any compartment $i$ and objective $k$ we have:
\begin{align*}
\sum_{(s_i,a_i)\in\mathcal{SA}_i}c_{i,k}(s_i\oplus a_i)\pi_i(s_i,a_i) 
&= \sum_{(s_i,a_i)\in\mathcal{SA}_i}\sum_{(\bm{s},\bm{a})\in\mathcal{SA}:[\bm{s},\bm{a}]_i=(s_i,a_i)}c_{i,k}(s_i\oplus a_i)\pi(\bm{s},\bm{a})\\
&= \sum_{\widehat{s_i,a_i}\in\widehat{\mathcal{SA}_i}}\sum_{(s_i,a_i)\in\widehat{s_i,a_i}}\sum_{(\bm{s},\bm{a})\in\mathcal{SA}:[\bm{s},\bm{a}]_i=(s_i,a_i)}c_{i,k}(s_i\oplus a_i)\pi(\bm{s},\bm{a})\\
&=\sum_{\widehat{s_i,a_i}\in\widehat{\mathcal{SA}_i}}c_{i,k}(\widehat{s_i,a_i})\sum_{(\bm{s},\bm{a})\in\mathcal{SA}:[\bm{s},\bm{a}]_i\in\widehat{s_i,a_i}}\pi(\bm{s},\bm{a})\\
&=\sum_{\widehat{s_i,a_i}\in\widehat{\mathcal{SA}_i}}c_{i,k}(\widehat{s_i,a_i})\sum_{\widehat{\bm{s},\bm{a}}\in\widehat{\mathcal{SA}}}\sum_{\bm{s},\bm{a}\in\widehat{s,a}:[\bm{s},\bm{a}]_i\in\widehat{s_i,a_i}}\pi(\bm{s},\bm{a})\\
&=\sum_{\widehat{s_i,a_i}\in\widehat{\mathcal{SA}_i}}c_{i,k}(\widehat{s_i,a_i})\sum_{\widehat{\bm{s},\bm{a}}\in\widehat{\mathcal{SA}}:[\widehat{\bm{s},\bm{a}}]_i=\widehat{s_i,a_i}}\widehat{\pi}(\widehat{\bm{s},\bm{a}})\\
&=\sum_{\widehat{s_i,a_i}\in\widehat{\mathcal{SA}_i}}c_{i,k}(\widehat{s_i,a_i})\widehat{\pi}_i(\widehat{s_i,a_i}).
\end{align*}
Therefore $\bm{g}(\bm{\pi})$ is entirely determined by the $\pi_i(\widehat{s_i,a_i})$ as determined by the equivalent solution to DC-MIP, so every solution to CS-MILP has a solution in DC-MIP with the same objective value.  

Secondly, we want to show the other direction. Let $(\bm{\pi}_i,\bm{y}_i)_{i=1}^I$ be a solution to DC-MIP. We want to show that it has a corresponding solution in CS-MILP with the same objective value. The solution $(\bm{\pi}_i,\bm{y}_i)_{i=1}^I$ can be mapped to a solution $(\bm{\pi},\bm{y})$ of CS-MILP by \autoref{prop:DC-MIP_to_CS-MILP}, with $\bm{\pi}$ and $\bm{\pi}_i$ related by \eqref{eq-whole-to-compartment-decision-vars} and \eqref{eq-compartment-to-whole-decision-vars}. Starting with the objective functions of DC-MIP, with $\bm{\pi}_i$ being the decision variables of DC-MIP (not the sum over variables of CS-MILP), we have:
    \begin{align*}
        \sum_{s_i,a_i\in\mathcal{SA}_i}c_{i,k}(s_i\oplus a_i)\pi_i(s_i,a_i) &= \sum_{\widehat{s_i,a_i}\in\widehat{\mathcal{SA}_i}}c_{i,k}(\widehat{s_i,a_i})\sum_{s_i,a_i\in\widehat{s_i,a_i}}\pi_i(s_i,a_i)\\
        &= \sum_{\widehat{s_i,a_i}\in\widehat{\mathcal{SA}_i}}c_{i,k}(\widehat{s_i,a_i})\widehat{\pi}_i(\widehat{s_i,a_i}),
    \end{align*}
    and we can then use the chain of equalities from the first part to get back to the objective function of CS-MILP, where the $\widehat{\pi}_i(\widehat{s_i,a_i})$ are determined by the $\widehat{\pi}(\widehat{\bm{s},\bm{a}})$, which in turn are determined by the equivalent solution to CS-MILP. Therefore every solution to DC-MIP has a solution in CS-MILP with the same objective value, and therefore the bi-implication holds.
